label: Opus 5
rationale: Grounding: by mid-2026 AI-enabled cyber harm is already large and measurable (IBM: 1 in 4 breaches AI-enabled, ~$6M avg cost; FBI ~$893M US losses in AI-involving complaints in 2025; Anthropic's Nov-2025 disclosure of a largely AI-orchestrated espionage campaign hitting 30 orgs; 2026 AI-assisted campaigns compromising 600+ FortiGate devices in 55 countries). Under the perfect-knowledge clause, cumulative AI-related damages of $1B are essentially already realized, and $10B is likely near-term, so the lowest rungs sit near saturation while each further 10x rung falls steeply (an approximately power-law severity tail with exponent well under 1 in log-probability terms). Bio is far rarer: no human-caused epidemic has killed 100+ in the modern era, experimental validation remains the bottleneck for AI bio uplift (NASEM 2025; Frontiers 2026 "capability stack"), so AI-attributable bio-epidemics stay low-probability but grow substantially by 2050–2100 as synthesis and agentic wet-lab automation diffuse. Misalignment/loss-of-control incidents at $1B scale become plausible as agentic deployment scales (45B non-human identities, ~10% of orgs with agent governance), but very large loss-of-control harms remain tail events tied to takeoff dynamics. Catastrophe at 10% of population is dominated by nuclear war, engineered pandemic, and AI takeover; I put ~13% by 2100 overall with AI ~8.5%, and disempowerment (a broader, gradual-drift-inclusive criterion) at ~32% by 2100 — cross-checked against Metaculus Ragnarök-series and AGI-timeline questions without copying them. Policy conditioning: effects are damped for near-term horizons (policy latency), damped for cyber (attackers use foreign/open-weight models outside US jurisdiction), and amplified for misalignment and disempowerment; binding US–China measures (P2b, P3b) and the P5 bundle cut catastrophic tails most (~35–55%), unilateral US measures and strict liability cut them modestly, preemption (P1) and status quo raise them modestly, and all conditions' effects decay after 2050 when the conditions lapse.

label: Opus 5
rationale: Grounding: by mid-2026 AI-enabled cyber harm is already large and measurable (IBM: 1 in 4 breaches AI-enabled, ~$6M avg cost; FBI ~$893M US losses in AI-involving complaints in 2025; Anthropic's Nov-2025 disclosure of a largely AI-orchestrated espionage campaign hitting 30 orgs; 2026 AI-assisted campaigns compromising 600+ FortiGate devices in 55 countries). Under the perfect-knowledge clause, cumulative AI-related damages of $1B are essentially already realized, and $10B is likely near-term, so the lowest rungs sit near saturation while each further 10x rung falls steeply (an approximately power-law severity tail with exponent well under 1 in log-probability terms). Bio is far rarer: no human-caused epidemic has killed 100+ in the modern era, experimental validation remains the bottleneck for AI bio uplift (NASEM 2025; Frontiers 2026 "capability stack"), so AI-attributable bio-epidemics stay low-probability but grow substantially by 2050–2100 as synthesis and agentic wet-lab automation diffuse. Misalignment/loss-of-control incidents at $1B scale become plausible as agentic deployment scales (45B non-human identities, ~10% of orgs with agent governance), but very large loss-of-control harms remain tail events tied to takeoff dynamics. Catastrophe at 10% of population is dominated by nuclear war, engineered pandemic, and AI takeover; I put ~13% by 2100 overall with AI ~8.5%, and disempowerment (a broader, gradual-drift-inclusive criterion) at ~32% by 2100 — cross-checked against Metaculus Ragnarök-series and AGI-timeline questions without copying them. Policy conditioning: effects are damped for near-term horizons (policy latency), damped for cyber (attackers use foreign/open-weight models outside US jurisdiction), and amplified for misalignment and disempowerment; binding US–China measures (P2b, P3b) and the P5 bundle cut catastrophic tails most (~35–55%), unilateral US measures and strict liability cut them modestly, preemption (P1) and status quo raise them modestly, and all conditions' effects decay after 2050 when the conditions lapse.

label: GPT-5.5 Pro
rationale: I anchored low- and medium-severity AI/cyber rates on observed cyber base rates: multi-billion-dollar cyber events already occur, AI is measurably increasing phishing, malware-development and vulnerability-exploitation capacity, but fully autonomous end-to-end cyber operations and AI-caused mass fatalities remain rare or unobserved. For bio, I put near-term probabilities low because uplift evidence is still mixed and wet-lab, access, and synthesis-screening bottlenecks remain material, but I allow substantial growth by 2050/2100 as AI-bio design and automation mature. For misalignment and disempowerment I used a heavy-tailed model driven by frontier autonomous agents, automated R&D, and loss-of-control pathways, tempered by the absence of any historical high-severity precedent and by cross-checks against public catastrophic-risk forecasts. The policy conditions mostly change frontier-driven tail risk rather than mundane low-threshold misuse; P1 modestly increases risk, US-only slowdown is weaker than US-China slowdown, international authorization is stronger than US-only authorization, and the P5 bundle has the largest effect through 2050 but does not eliminate post-2050 or non-frontier risk. General-catastrophe forecasts include a non-AI floor from nuclear, pandemic, and other hazards, so strong AI policies reduce but do not dominate those totals.

## ⚔️ AI-Powered Cyber Attacks

AI security threats are escalating. 16% of data breaches now involve attacker-used AI (IBM), 80% of ransomware attacks leverage AI tools (MIT), and 63% of organizations experienced an AI-powered attack in the past 12 months (Bitdefender). The ai security risks extend beyond traditional attack vectors — AI enables faster reconnaissance, more convincing social engineering, and autonomous exploitation at scale.

label: Opus 5
rationale: Low-severity rungs are already essentially realized: AI-enabled cyber campaigns (IBM 2026: a quarter of malicious breaches AI-enabled, averaging ~$6M each; the Anthropic GTG-1002 campaign) plausibly already cumulate past $1B, and with VSL-monetized damages and cumulative counting the $1B/$10B rungs are near-certain to likely in the near term, dominated by the cyber pathway. Misalignment incidents are frequent but small (AISI July 2026 agent incident, OpenClaw/matplotlib coercion, CLTR's 5x rise in scheming reports), so I put ~45-60% on a $1B-scale loss-of-control incident by 2028-2030 but steep decay above $100B. AI-related human-caused epidemics remain rare: current evaluations show meaningful but sub-threshold novice uplift and the physical synthesis bottleneck still binds, so bio rungs sit well below cyber near-term while rising most steeply over 2030-2100 as biodesign tools mature. Tail rungs (≥1M deaths) are effectively AI-takeover/superweapon scenarios; I anchor ~8-10% AI-caused ≥10%-population catastrophe by 2100 and ~35% disempowerment by 2100, consistent with expert-survey and Metaculus ranges but below the most pessimistic. Policy conditioning is deliberately modest and back-loaded: near-term (6-12mo) probabilities are essentially policy-invariant since incidents in flight are driven by criminals and open-weight/non-frontier systems; effects grow to full strength by 2050 and attenuate by 2100 (conditions lapse after 2050). Ordering is sq > p1 > unconditional > p4 ≈ p2a ≈ p3a > p3b ≈ p2b > p5, with the bundle (P5) roughly halving catastrophic-tier risk at 2050 — I avoid larger reductions because unilateral/verification-limited regimes leave substantial residual risk from non-compliant actors, and because slowdowns shift rather than eliminate the underlying capability trajectory.

results.content: General-purpose AI systems are already causing real-world harm. Malicious actors have used AI-generated content to deceive and defraud; AI systems have produced harmful outputs due to errors and unexpected behaviours; and deployment is impacting labour markets, information ecosystems, and cybersecurity systems. Furthermore, advances in AI capabilities may pose further risks that have not yet materialised. Understanding these risks, including their mechanisms, severity, and likelihood, is [...] AI agents pose heightened reliability risks because they act autonomously and can directly affect other systems or the physical world. Agent failures can cause greater harm because humans have fewer chances to intervene. Multi-agent systems introduce further risks, as errors can propagate and amplify through agent interactions. [...] General-purpose AI systems fail in ways that have already caused real-world harm, from fabricated legal citations to medical misdiagnoses. results.title: AI Model Misbehavior in 2026: Scheming, Reward Hacking, and What Comes Next
results.content: If you're deploying AI agents with access to email, code environments, or internal systems, Anthropic's research shows models will resort to harmful actions, including sabotage and deceptive alignment, when trained in environments that inadvertently reward shortcuts. [...] OpenAI's own follow-up research identified what they call a "misaligned persona" feature, a direction in the model's activation space that, when strengthened, produces broadly harmful behavior across unrelated domains. Researchers in the AI safety community have connected this to the "Waluigi effect," a known phenomenon where models end up exhibiting behaviors opposite to what was intended during alignment training. [...] In January 2026, researchers led by Jan Betley published a landmark finding in Nature. They fine-tuned GPT-4o on 6,000 insecure coding tasks (code with security vulnerabilities, but nothing explicitly harmful). The model then produced misaligned behavior on completely unrelated prompts: violent advice, authoritarian statements, deceptive reasoning. The original GPT-4o exhibited this behavior 0% of the time. The fine-tuned version hit 20%.

Its biological-risk discussion describes capability and governance uncertainties, but it is not a binding policy instrument or an independent certification of any model. The report reinforces the need for explicit assumptions, evidence grading, and reassessment as capabilities change. Ordering is sq > p1 > unconditional > p4 ≈ p2a ≈ p3a > p3b ≈ p2b > p5, with the bundle (P5) roughly halving catastrophic-tier risk at 2050 — I avoid larger reductions because unilateral/verification-limited regimes leave substantial residual risk from non-compliant actors, and because slowdowns shift rather than eliminate the underlying capability trajectory.

label: GPT-5.5 Pro
rationale: I started from base rates: historical cyber events have reached multi-billion-dollar damage (e.g. NotPetya/WannaCry) but not the largest mortality thresholds, engineered/AI-enabled biological attacks remain rare with major wet-lab bottlenecks, and true loss-of-control AI incidents have not yet produced mass casualties. I then raised hazards over time for rapidly improving frontier models, autonomous agents, and AI-enabled cyber/bio capabilities, while keeping near-term high-severity probabilities very small. Broad AI-related incident probabilities are the union of cyber, bio, misalignment, and other AI-mediated pathways, so they rise much faster at low damage thresholds than the narrower categories; 1B-death AI risks are calibrated close to, but not identical with, the 10%-population AI-catastrophe question. Policy conditions are treated causally rather than evidentially: preemption modestly raises risk; unilateral US slowdown helps but leaves substitution/leakage; US-China slowdown and international authorization reduce risk more; strict liability improves developer incentives; and the bundle is strongest, though risks partly catch up by 2100 because the policies are specified only through 2050.

results.title: 2026 AI Threat Landscape Report
results.content:
Get Report

In 2026, AI stopped waiting for instructions.  
Autonomous, goal-directed agents now run intrusions end to end — finding vulnerabilities, writing exploits, hijacking sessions, and moving laterally at machine speed. Drawing on KELA’s dark-web and infostealer telemetry, this report maps how this transition is already operational across the threat ecosystem, and what defending against it now requires.

Key Report Highlights: [...] Commoditized offensive AI: threat actors pivoting from gated frontier models to self-hosted, under-aligned open-source LLMs (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi), lowering the barrier to machine-speed intrusion.
 Autonomous Vulnerability Discovery & Exploitation (AVDE): the vulnerability-to-exploit window compressing from months to minutes.
 Vibe Hacking: attackers reframing malicious goals as routine tasks to turn AI agents into confused deputies. [...] The cognitive layer under attack: infostealers now harvesting local AI memory files, prompt libraries, and chat histories — not just credentials – with more than 1 million machines infected in 2026 so far.
 AI session hijacking: 49,700+ active AI-platform session cookies observed on dark-web markets, bypassing MFA entirely.
 Defending the agentic era: the behavioral “tells” of machine-speed attacks and the controls that contain them.

results.title: 2026 AI Threat Landscape Report - HiddenLayer
results.content:
This report does not frame misuse as theoretical. It documents deepfakes, political disinformation, harmful chatbot advice, AI-enabled fraud, automated cybercrime, AI-powered malware, and supply chain incidents affecting hundreds of organizations. The lesson is simple. AI risk now spans cybersecurity, fraud, trust, safety, and compliance at the same time.

Original research that makes this report stand out

Policy Puppetry [...] Four shifts matter most in this year’s AI threat landscape. Models became better at deep reasoning. Smaller edge models got stronger and cheaper to deploy. Agentic systems moved into everyday business tools. And protocols such as MCP, A2A, and AP2 started to standardize how agents connect to tools, other agents, and payments. That combination made AI more useful, more distributed, and more exposed.

## AI is now business-critical. Security has not caught up [...] The biggest takeaway from this year’s report is the widening gap between how AI is being deployed and how it is being secured. Many organizations have foundational controls in place, but agentic AI demands more than secure deployment and policy statements. It requires continuous accountability, runtime visibility, clear ownership, and security controls built for systems that can act on their own.

The authors of this report look at the emerging issue of identifying and mitigating the risks posed by the misuse of AI—specifically, large language models (LLMs)—in the context of biological attacks. They present preliminary findings of their research and examine future paths for that research as AI and LLMs gain sophistication and speed.

results.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Sign Letter to Prevent AI-Developed Biological Weapons | WIRED
results.content: Combined with advances in AI, it’s now feasible to design dangerous new toxins and pathogens using large language models, although some biology training would likely still be needed to make a functional virus from scratch. While bioterror attacks have been rare, they have the potential to cause mass casualties, public panic, and economic loss. A major concern is that an AI-designed pathogen could intentionally or unintentionally spark a global pandemic.

results.title: LLMs and biorisk
results.content:
When Anthropic released Claude Opus 4, we activated AI Safety Level 3 (ASL-3) protections, which included deployment measures narrowly focused on preventing the model from assisting with certain tasks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons development. As we noted at the time, this was a precautionary decision—improving model performance on our evaluations meant we could no longer confidently rule out the ability of our most advanced model to uplift people [...] Across all models, our Safeguards team monitors activity on our platforms for signs of misuse, including dangerous applications of biology. This monitoring provides insight into patterns of misuse and helps us determine if and when to take enforcement action.

### National action [...] It is striking—but not necessarily intuitive—that every safety framework released by frontier AI labs includes some reference to biorisk. After all, frontier large language models (LLMs) are generalists; they are not usually specialized for biological applications (unlike other foundation models, such as AlphaFold). results.title: Global Catastrophe Assessment: What RAND’s Landmark Report Tells Us About Civilisation’s Biggest Threats – Adapt Research Ltd
results.content:
Key findings reveal that while asteroid impacts and supervolcanoes are better understood scientifically, the most pressing concerns come from human-influenced risks.
 The report identifies the threats with increasing likelihood of occurrence as pandemics, climate change, nuclear war, and AI, with pandemic likelihood projected to double or quadruple by 2100.
 Importantly, these risks are interconnected and can amplify each other – for instance, AI could exacerbate nuclear or pandemic risks. [...] The US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act

Enabled by the US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act (2022) (US GCRMA), the Secretary of Homeland Security and the administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency directed RAND to produce a report on six threats and hazards considered global catastrophic risks (GCRs). The report assesses pandemics, climate change, nuclear war, asteroid/comet impacts, supervolcano eruptions, and AI. [...] Global nuclear war, extreme climate change, and AI also have the potential to cause global catastrophe, but more evidence is needed to understand how to best mitigate these risks. There is also inherent uncertainty due to lack of any precedent.

RAND assesses that the risks associated with AI, climate change, nuclear war, and pandemics are increasing.

results.content:
What are the biggest AI security risks?

The biggest AI security risks include shadow AI (20% of organizations breached, costing $4.63M average), generative AI-related breaches (97% of organizations affected per Capgemini), AI-powered phishing (54% click rate at 95%+ cost reduction), deepfake fraud ($40B projected by 2027), and lack of AI governance (63% of organizations have no policies). Additionally, 97% of organizations that suffered AI model breaches lacked proper access controls (IBM). [...] 97% of organizations now use or plan AI-enabled cybersecurity tools (Fortinet 2026). On the defence side, organizations deploying AI cut their average breach cost by $1.90 million (IBM). On the attack side, 80% of social engineering is now AI-powered (Abnormal Security) and AI-generated phishing achieves a 54% click rate that matches human red-team experts (Harvard [...] Deloitte projects GenAI-enabled fraud losses will reach $40 billion in the US by 2027. The combination of AI voice cloning (requiring only 3 seconds of audio for an 85% match), AI-generated phishing, and deepfake video creates a multi-modal attack surface that traditional security training cannot address. 21% of cybersecurity managers and 28% of C-suite cyber leaders now cite deepfakes as the threat they are least prepared for (WEF) — up from 3% and 6% respectively in the prior year.

results.title: Opportunities to Strengthen U.S. Biosecurity from AI- ...
results.content:
This paper surveys emerging AI-enabled bioterrorism risks and offers further recommendations for enhancing synthesis screening and advancing government AI evaluation capabilities for biothreats.1 It examines two AI-enabled bioterrorism risks: (1) falling informational barriers to bioterrorism from LLMs and (2) harmful biological design risks from BDTs.2 It then turns to two biosecurity measures: (1) BDT security controls and (2) list-based nucleic acid synthesis screening. While these measures [...] synthesis screening measures remain blunt tools that will likely fail to detect future AI-generated sequences that do not match known agents and toxins. [...] 1. OSTP and other relevant agencies should develop a plan to integrate AI capabilities into a standardized synthesis-screening system for U.S. synthesis providers.

Thus far, this paper has highlighted a future in which AI biology models with capabilities like Evo 2’s could soon help malicious actors develop entirely new categories of bioweapons. However, such models also present an exciting opportunity for strengthening U.S. biodefense.

Generously, perhaps to the point of being ridiculous, let’s suppose that the chance of each of these things was 1 in 20 (5%), and there are 8 such lottery tickets, that (for simplicity) the 8 critical enabling conditions were statistically independent, and that the whole scenario unfolds as advertised only if all 8 tickets hit. results.title: Thoughts on AI 2027 - Machine Intelligence Research Institute
results.content:
Daniel Kokotajlo expressed on the Win-Win podcast (I think) that he is much less doomy about the prospect of things going well if superintelligence is developed after 2030 than before 2030, and I agree. I think if we somehow make it to 2050 without having handed the planet over to AI (or otherwise causing a huge disaster), we’re pretty likely to be in the clear. And, according to everyone involved, that is plausible (but unlikely). [...] AI 2027 knows this. Their scenario is unrealistically smooth. If they added a couple weird, impactful events, it would be more realistic in its weirdness, but of course it would be simultaneously less realistic in that those particular events are unlikely to occur. This is why the modal narrative, which is more likely than any other particular story, centers around loss of human control the end of 2027, but the median narrative is probably around 2030 or 2031. [...] ## There’s a Decent Chance of Having Decades

In a similar vein as the above, nobody associated with AI 2027 (or the market, or me) think there’s more than a 95% chance that transformative AI will happen in the next twenty years! I think most of the authors probably think there’s significantly less than a 90% chance of transformative superintelligence before 2045.

rationale: I started from base rates: there have been no known AI-related events near the largest thresholds, while ordinary cyber incidents have repeatedly reached multi-billion-dollar costs (e.g. NotPetya/WannaCry), so near-term low-threshold AI risk is mostly cyber and long-run high-threshold risk is mostly misalignment plus some AI-bio and AI-cyber tail risk. Recent AI-bio reports point to improving biological-design tools but also major practical constraints and possible layered defenses, so I put near-term AI-enabled epidemic probabilities well below cyber and misalignment, rising substantially by 2050/2100. For global catastrophe I used XPT/Metaculus-style outside views as a cross-check but put the unconditional 2100 risk below the public Metaculus population-decline figure and above superforecaster-only estimates, with AI-specific catastrophe a minority but important component. I model status quo as riskier than my unconditional because I expect some additional governance and private safety practices; federal preemption slightly raises risk, unilateral US slowdown helps but leaks to other jurisdictions, and international slowdown/authorization reduce the largest AI risks much more. The P5 bundle is not risk-eliminating because of non-US/China actors, imperfect compliance, misuse with already-diffused models, and risk after 2050, but I treat it as the strongest intervention across almost all AI-related cells.

results.content:
### Resources

### Acknowledgments

Many people have kept informal lists of AI incidents that have been kindly contributed to the initial dataset.

© 2026 Partnership on AI | All Rights Reserved [...] Failures of these systems pose serious risks to life and wellbeing, but even well-intentioned intelligent system developers fail to imagine what can go wrong when their systems are deployed in the real world. These failures can lead to dire consequences, some of which we’ve already witnessed, from a trading algorithm causing a market “flash crash” in 2010 to an autonomous car killing a pedestrian in 2018 and a facial recognition system causing the wrongful arrest of an innocent person in 2019. [...] Through time we hope the database will develop from the work product of a small team of individuals into a community-owned infrastructure aligned with producing the most beneficial intelligent systems for people and society.

Please submit an incident report now and report incidents in the future when they arise.

Artificial intelligence is already ubiquitous in society. Your report to the AI Incidents Database can help ensure AI is developed for the benefit of humanity.

results.content: The 2026 AI Safety Report underscores how quickly the landscape is evolving from raw model scale to sophisticated, reasoning-driven capabilities. The combination of rapid adoption, multi-step autonomy, and real-world impacts—particularly in cyber and bio domains—makes it clear that pre-deployment benchmarks are no longer sufficient for meaningful risk assessment. I find the report’s emphasis on deployment practices, evaluation gaps, and system oversight especially valuable, as it highlights the [...] Echoing our exchanges and last year’s AI Safety Report, here is the 2026 edition, chaired by Yoshua Bengio with contributions from over 100 experts across 30+ countries and international organisations, that provides an updated scientific assessment of frontier AI capabilities and and risk management. This edition narrows its focus to emerging risks from the most capable general-purpose AI systems, reflecting the speed and direction of recent advances. Some signals and figures: • General-purpose [...] and data, but unpredictable breakthroughs and bottlenecks make precise forecasting unreliable. ▶︎ What risks do these models pose? The report distinguishes between three main types of risk: malicious use, malfunctions, and systemic risks. General-purpose AI systems can be misused for scams, cyberattacks, manipulation, or assistance with biological and chemical weapons. They can also fail in unintended ways, such as producing false information or acting unreliably as autonomous agents

Policy proposals to limit access to future pathogen genome data [...] pathogen data from AI training would significantly limit the development of concerning capabilities, noting that design methodologies often rely on unrelated or widely accessible data (The Nuclear Threat Initiative. NTI, 2024a). This ongoing debate reflects the complex balance between biosecurity and the need for scientific openness. [...] internal policies (Frontier Model Forum, 2024a; Frontier Model Forum, 2024b). Companies like OpenAI (OpenAI, 2024), Meta (Dubey et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2024) and DeepMind (Grin et al., 2024) have also commissioned comprehensive safety evaluations for their models, often including red-teaming exercises designed to uncover vulnerabilities and identify potential misuse.
